title: 26 U.S. Code Section 41(d)(4) Excluded Activities
description: 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4) lists eight categories of activity excluded from the federal R&D credit even when the work passes the four-part test.
summary: 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4) lists eight categories of activity excluded from the federal R&D tax credit, even when work passes the four-part test: research after commercial production, adaptation, duplication, surveys and routine testing, internal use software, foreign research, social sciences or humanities, and funded research. U.S. taxpayers must substantiate that claimed QREs avoid these exclusions.

body.text: 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4) lists eight categories of activity excluded from the federal R&D tax credit, even when work passes the four-part test: research after commercial production, adaptation, duplication, surveys and routine testing, internal use software, foreign research, social sciences or humanities, and funded research. U.S. taxpayers must substantiate that claimed QREs avoid these exclusions.
Statutory Architecture of 26 U.S. Code Section 41(d)(4)

Section 41(d)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)) functions as a mandatory statutory exclusion filter within the federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit regime. While the federal research credit is structured to lower the after-tax cost of domestic technological innovation, Congress restricted its scope to prevent routine commercial operations, ordinary production runs, and standard business administration from being subsidized as qualified research. Under the statutory framework of 26 U.S.C. § 41, a taxpayer's activities must first satisfy the foundational four-part test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) at the individual business component level. Specifically, the activity must involve expenditures eligible for treatment as specified research or experimental expenditures under 26 U.S.C. § 174 (the Section 174 eligibility test), be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature by relying on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science (the technological in nature test), be intended for application in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer while seeking the elimination of technical uncertainty concerning capability, method, or appropriate design (the business component and uncertainty test), and entail activities substantially all of which constitute elements of a process of experimentation related to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality (the process of experimentation test). However, satisfying the affirmative four-part test under Section 41(d)(1) is legally insufficient on its own; Section 41(d)(4) overrides initial technical eligibility and categorically disqualifies eight enumerated classes of activity regardless of their underlying scientific or engineering complexity.

The operational consequence of this two-tier statutory architecture is that qualification disputes in federal and state tax examinations rarely turn solely on whether engineers, metallurgists, or computer scientists performed complex technical work. Instead, administrative disallowances by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and appellate litigation before the federal circuit courts frequently focus on whether otherwise technical activities have crossed the temporal boundary into post-commercial production under Section 41(d)(4)(A), constitute customer-specific adaptation of an existing design under Section 41(d)(4)(B), replicate existing technical specifications under Section 41(d)(4)(C), represent internal general and administrative software development failing the elevated regulatory threshold under Section 41(d)(4)(E), occur outside the geographic territory of the United States under Section 41(d)(4)(F), or shift financial risk to a third party as funded research under Section 41(d)(4)(H).

A critical structural effect of this statutory framework is that the Section 41(d)(4) exclusions create an asymmetric burden of proof during tax examinations. Because tax credits are a matter of legislative grace, a corporate taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of proving not only that a business component satisfied the four-part test of Section 41(d)(1), but also that no portion of the claimed qualified research expenses (QREs) bled into an excluded phase or category under Section 41(d)(4). When project accounting systems capture engineering labor at the broad department or cost-center level rather than tracking discrete sub-component milestones, the presence of excluded post-production debugging or customer adaptation can taint the entire cost pool, preventing the taxpayer from establishing a reasonable basis for the 80% "substantially all" experimentation threshold. Understanding the precise statutory, regulatory, and judicial contours of these eight exclusions is therefore essential for corporate taxpayers seeking to substantiate eligible claims while mitigating federal and state audit exposure.
Legislative Evolution and Section 174 Capitalization Linkage

The federal research tax credit was originally enacted in mid-1981 under the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (ERTA) as a temporary fiscal incentive aimed at stimulating business investment in basic and applied industrial research. Because the original statutory language lacked a rigorous definition of research and was broad enough to permit taxpayers to claim tax credits for standard product development, seasonal style changes, and minor commercial modifications, Congress enacted the Tax Reform Act of 1986 to narrow the definition of "qualified research" to genuine technological experimentation and expressly codified the statutory exclusions now found in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4). The legislative design of the 1986 amendments established a bright-line statutory demarcation separating experimental research aimed at resolving fundamental technical uncertainty from the ordinary business costs of commercializing, adapting, or duplicating existing technologies.

Following the 1986 statutory overhaul, Congress repeatedly modified and extended the credit through a series of temporary enactments—including the Revenue Reconciliation Act of 1989, the Small Business Job Protection Act of 1996, the Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997, the Tax and Trade Relief Extension Act of 1998, and the Tax Relief Extension Act of 1999—before permanently codifying the credit in the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015. Administrative enforcement of these statutory amendments culminated in the promulgation of final Treasury Regulations on January 3, 2001 (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4, T.D. 8930, 66 FR 280), alongside subsequent regulatory refinements addressing the uncertainty standard and internal use software. Those regulations clarified a critical doctrinal balance: while qualified research encompasses evolutionary technological advances and does not demand that a taxpayer be the first in its industry to achieve a revolutionary breakthrough, the regulatory framework strictly bars activities that adapt, duplicate, or refine a business component after it achieves commercial readiness.

Established the temporary federal research tax credit for basic and applied research without the detailed exclusion framework later codified in Section 41(d)(4).
Tax Reform Act of 1986
Narrowed the definition of "qualified research" and introduced the explicit statutory exclusions codified in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4) to bar routine business and commercial development costs.
Interim Statutory Refinements

Modified and extended the administrative boundaries of the credit through the Revenue Reconciliation Act of 1989, Small Business Job Protection Act of 1996, Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997, Tax and Trade Relief Extension Act of 1998, and Tax Relief Extension Act of 1999.
Final Treasury Regulations (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4)
January 3, 2001

Standardized regulatory enforcement of Section 41(d)(4)(A)–(H) exclusions under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c), confirming eligibility for evolutionary advances while barring post-commercialization refinement, adaptation, and duplication.
Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act
Made the federal research credit and its accompanying Section 41(d)(4) exclusion structure permanent within the Internal Revenue Code.
Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) § 174 Amendments
Effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021

Mandated capitalization and amortization of Section 174 research and experimental expenditures over 5 years (domestic) and 15 years (foreign), elevating the cash-flow consequences of distinguishing Section 41(d)(4) excluded commercial activities from research.

body.text: The statutory interaction between 26 U.S.C. § 41 and 26 U.S.C. § 174 assumed heightened financial significance under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA). For tax years beginning after December 31, 2021, the TCJA amendments to Section 174 eliminated the historical option to immediately expense research and experimental costs, mandating instead that taxpayers capitalize and amortize domestic research and experimental expenditures over a five-year period and foreign research expenditures over a 15-year period. Because Section 41(d)(1)(A) defines qualified research by direct reference to expenditures treatable as specified research or experimental expenditures under Section 174, the boundary lines established by Section 41(d)(4) carry dual compliance and cash-flow consequences.

A compounding financial risk emerges from this statutory linkage between Section 174 capitalization and Section 41(d)(4) exclusions. Prior to 2022, when corporate taxpayers could deduct both ordinary business expenses under 26 U.S.C. § 162 and research expenditures under 26 U.S.C. § 174 in full during the year incurred, the primary risk of claiming an overbroad Section 41 credit was the disallowance of the incremental credit itself. Under the post-2021 TCJA regime, however, misclassifying routine commercial production, post-deployment debugging, or customer adaptation costs as research exposes corporate taxpayers to severe audit and cash-flow exposure: the IRS can disallow the Section 41 credit under the specific exclusions of Section 41(d)(4) while simultaneously scrutinizing whether the taxpayer properly segregated ordinary Section 162 trade or business expenses from capitalized Section 174 pools, or worse, trapping foreign subcontracted engineering costs in a mandatory 15-year amortization schedule under Section 174 while barring any offsetting tax credit under Section 41(d)(4)(F).
Analysis of the Eight Statutory Exclusions Under Section 41(d)(4)

Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c) articulates the administrative definitions, operational mechanics, and illustrative examples for each of the eight excluded activity categories enumerated in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A) through (H). Across all eight provisions, the regulatory framework enforces a consistent policy objective: terminating tax credit eligibility at the boundary where the experimental resolution of scientific or engineering uncertainty gives way to commercial execution, routine customization, geographic offshoring, or general administrative operations.

headers: Regulatory Scope Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c) and Related Rules

cells: Research After Commercial Production

Activities conducted after a business component meets the basic functional and economic requirements of the taxpayer or is ready for commercial sale or use, including post-production troubleshooting and debugging.
Engineering time claimed after Critical Design Review (CDR) or after the initial commercial production run without a new Engineering Change Proposal (ECP).
Adaptation of an Existing Business Component
Activities relating to adapting an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need where no new fundamental technological uncertainty exists.
Customizing spatial dimensions, interfaces, or known engineering parameters for a specific client contract.
Duplication of an Existing Business Component
Reproduction of an existing business component, in whole or in part, from physical examination, plans, blueprints, or detailed specifications, including reverse engineering.
Replicating a competitor's product or manufacturing process rather than generating new technical information.
Surveys, Studies, and Routine Testing
Efficiency surveys, management studies, market research, routine data collection, and routine quality control testing or inspection.
Including standard production quality assurance or operational efficiency studies in qualified research pools.
Internal Use Software
Software developed primarily for internal general and administrative (G&A) functions (payroll, human resources, accounting), unless it satisfies the three-part High Threshold of Innovation Test.
Internal enterprise automation or AI tools that customize existing software without substantial economic risk or measurable leaps in speed or cost.
Foreign Research
Research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any U.S. possession; also subject to 15-year amortization under 26 U.S.C. § 174.
Subcontracting CAD modeling, testing, or software engineering to offshore entities, even when results are analyzed in the United States.
Social Sciences, Arts, or Humanities
Any research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities, restricting the credit exclusively to engineering, computer science, biological, or physical sciences.
Behavioral, economic, aesthetic, or market-oriented studies lacking hard-science experimentation.
Funded Research

Research funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity, evaluated by whether payment is contingent on technical success and whether the taxpayer retains substantial rights.
Time-and-materials or capped cost-plus contracts, or commercial agreements with standard warranty inspection clauses where the client bears financial risk.

body.text: Research After Commercial Production Under Section 41(d)(4)(A)

Codified at 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A) and detailed in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(2), the exclusion for research after commercial production imposes a strict chronological cutoff on qualified research. Under the regulatory standard, activities conducted after the beginning of commercial production of a business component are per se excluded from the credit. A business component is deemed to have reached the beginning of commercial production when it has been developed to the point where it either meets the basic functional and economic requirements of the taxpayer for the component's sale or use, or is otherwise ready for commercial sale or use. Once that functional and economic threshold is crossed, the experimental phase terminates as a matter of law, and subsequent engineering activities are excluded regardless of their technical difficulty. Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(c)(2) specifically enumerates activities treated as occurring after commercial production, including pre-production planning for a finished business component, tooling-up for production, trial production runs, trouble-shooting involving detecting faults in production equipment or processes, accumulating data relating to production processes, and debugging flaws in a business component after commercial deployment.

The IRS Aerospace Industry Research Credit Audit Technique Guide (ATG, issued in 2005) illustrates how field examiners operationalize Section 41(d)(4)(A) during technical audits of complex manufacturing and engineering programs. In aerospace and defense engineering programs, system development progresses through structured stage-gate milestones from Preliminary Design Review (PDR) to Critical Design Review (CDR). During the PDR phase, technical adequacy, system architecture, and early engineering progress are evaluated amid substantial uncertainty regarding capability and design; consequently, design engineering activities leading up to PDR generally satisfy the experimental requirements for the credit. By contrast, CDR occurs immediately prior to manufacturing approval and evaluates final cost, schedule, and performance compliance against fixed specifications. Once a project clears CDR, the engineering design is functionally "frozen". Consequently, the IRS Aerospace ATG instructs field examiners and IRS engineers to closely scrutinize and challenge any research credit claims for engineering hours incurred after CDR because the business component is transitioning directly into commercial production and manufacturing execution.

Similarly, if a manufacturer accelerates an initial design to market and initiates its first commercial production run, the research phase legally ends upon that initial production run. Post-production troubleshooting, routine operational data collection, and standard engineering debugging to resolve minor operational flaws or customer complaints are categorically barred under Section 41(d)(4)(A). The sole recognized exception occurs when a clinical or manufacturing failure reveals a fundamental design defect that forces the taxpayer to halt production and initiate a fundamentally new design phase—such as issuing a formal Engineering Change Proposal (ECP) in an aerospace program—that introduces new technological uncertainty requiring an independent process of experimentation. Even in that scenario, only the incremental experimental redesign activities aimed at resolving the newly discovered technological uncertainty qualify, rather than the routine manufacturing adjustments accompanying the rollout.
Adaptation, Duplication, Surveys, Foreign Research, and Social Sciences Under Sections 41(d)(4)(B)–(D), (F), and (G)

Sections 41(d)(4)(B) and 41(d)(4)(C), implemented via Treas. Reg. §§ 1.41-4(c)(3) and (c)(4), operate in tandem to exclude the adaptation and duplication of existing business components. The adaptation exclusion under Section 41(d)(4)(B) disqualifies engineering, manufacturing, or software integration work that modifies an existing business component to satisfy a particular customer's requirement or need when no new fundamental technological uncertainty is present. Even where customization demands highly skilled engineering labor, complex computer-aided design (CAD) scaling, or site-specific system integration, reconfiguring known scientific and engineering parameters to fit a specific client's spatial layout, weight tolerance, or software environment constitutes an excluded adaptation because the underlying uncertainty is commercial and logistical rather than technological. Similarly, the duplication exclusion under Section 41(d)(4)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(4) bars the reproduction of an existing business component, in whole or in part, from a physical examination of the business component itself or from plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information with respect to such component. While the regulation notes that examining an existing component in the course of developing a different component with new functional characteristics is not automatically barred, Section 41(d)(4)(C) expressly disqualifies reverse engineering of a competitor's product or manufacturing process because extracting existing technical information does not generate new scientific knowledge to eliminate technological uncertainty.

Section 41(d)(4)(D) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(5) exclude efficiency surveys, activities relating to management functions or techniques, market research, testing, or development (including advertising or promotions), routine data collection, and routine or ordinary testing or inspection for quality control. This provision prevents taxpayers from sweeping industrial engineering time-and-motion studies, lean manufacturing reorganizations, consumer focus groups, or end-of-line quality assurance (QA) batch testing into the research credit calculation. While destructive testing of experimental prototypes during pre-production design qualifies as part of a process of experimentation, routine validation testing performed to verify that commercial units conform to established specifications is strictly excluded.

Section 41(d)(4)(F) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(7) exclude any research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States. This geographic exclusion is determined strictly by the physical location where the research activities are performed, rather than the residence of the taxpayer, the domicile of the paying corporate entity, or the jurisdiction where the resulting intellectual property is owned. Consequently, if a domestic corporation subcontracts CAD modeling, finite element analysis, or software coding to an engineering vendor or corporate subsidiary physically located in a foreign country, those offshore expenditures are 100% excluded under Section 41(d)(4)(F), even if the resulting engineering data files are transmitted back to the United States and subsequently evaluated by domestic engineers. Furthermore, such foreign research expenditures are subjected to a 15-year mandatory amortization recovery period under 26 U.S.C. § 174(a)(2)(B), creating a pronounced tax drag on offshore R&D subcontracting. Finally, Section 41(d)(4)(G) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(8) exclude all research in the social sciences (including economics, business management, and behavioral sciences), arts, or humanities, confining credit eligibility strictly to the hard sciences—namely engineering, computer science, biological sciences, and physical sciences.
Internal Use Software and the High Threshold of Innovation Under Section 41(d)(4)(E)

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(E) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6), computer software developed by (or for the benefit of) the taxpayer primarily for internal use is statutorily excluded from qualified research unless it falls within narrow statutory exceptions (such as software developed for use in an activity that itself constitutes qualified research or for use in a qualified production process) or satisfies an elevated regulatory standard known as the High Threshold of Innovation Test. Under the Treasury Regulations, software is presumed to be developed primarily for internal use if it is developed for use in general and administrative (G&A) functions that facilitate or support the conduct of the taxpayer's trade or business—specifically including financial management, accounting, payroll, human resources management, and support services functions—rather than being developed to be commercially sold, leased, licensed, or otherwise marketed to third parties, or to enable the taxpayer to interact with third parties or allow third parties to initiate functions or review data on the taxpayer's system.

To overcome the Section 41(d)(4)(E) exclusion, internal use software must not only fulfill the foundational four-part test of Section 41(d)(1), but must also simultaneously satisfy all three cumulative conditions of the High Threshold of Innovation Test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6). First, the software must be innovative, meaning that the software is intended to result in a substantial and economically significant reduction in cost, improvement in speed, or other measurable improvement that is substantial and economically significant, rather than merely offering customized user workflows, interface updates, or visual enhancements. Second, the software development must involve significant economic risk, wherein the taxpayer commits substantial resources to the development and faces substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that such resources would be recovered within a reasonable period. Third, the software must be commercially unavailable for use by the taxpayer, meaning that the software cannot be purchased, leased, or licensed and used for the intended purpose without modifications that would themselves satisfy the innovation and significant economic risk requirements.

In contemporary IRS Large Business and International (LB&I) examination practice, field specialists apply this three-part exclusion test with heightened skepticism to internal artificial intelligence (AI) deployments, enterprise resource planning (ERP) migrations, and back-office automation projects. Examiners routinely treat enterprise software implementations and internal machine-learning wrappers as excluded G&A software under Section 41(d)(4)(E) unless the taxpayer can prove that the underlying computer science architecture achieved a demonstrable, quantifiable leap in computational speed or cost reduction while confronting genuine technical risk rather than mere implementation or configuration challenges. Moreover, financial accounting standards promulgated by the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) under Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) 350-40 (Internal-Use Software) and ASC 730 (Research and Development) maintain parallel conceptual boundaries on software and research costs. In alignment with IRS LB&I examination guidance, the excluded activities across ASC 730, IRC § 174, and IRC § 41 are broadly harmonized in excluding routine selling, general and administrative operations, and periodic minor alterations to existing products or systems from the definition of research.
Funded Research and Contractual Allocation of Risk Under Section 41(d)(4)(H)

Section 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(9) (incorporating the regulatory standards of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)) exclude any research to the extent it is funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or governmental entity. The statutory objective of the funded research exclusion is twofold: to prevent multiple entities (such as both a contractor and its customer) from claiming the R&D tax credit for the same underlying expenditures, and to allocate the tax incentive exclusively to the party that actually bears the financial risk of technical failure. Under the governing regulatory framework, when a taxpayer performs research for a client or government agency under contract, the research is deemed funded—and therefore categorically excluded for the contractor under Section 41(d)(4)(H)—unless the contractor simultaneously establishes two distinct legal conditions from the four corners of the executed contract. First, the amounts payable under the agreement must be strictly contingent upon the technical success of the research (the payment contingency requirement). Second, the taxpayer performing the research must retain substantial rights in the research results, meaning the taxpayer is not stripped of the right to use or exploit the resulting technology in its own trade or business without paying a royalty to the client (the substantial rights requirement).

The interplay of these two conditions makes contractual drafting and billing structure the decisive determinants of credit eligibility for engineering firms, defense contractors, and custom manufacturers. Contracts structured around time-and-materials (T&M) billing, cost-reimbursable terms, or fixed hourly reimbursement without an explicit contractual condition tying payment to ultimate technical success place the financial risk of failed experimentation on the client, automatically disqualifying the contractor under Section 41(d)(4)(H). Conversely, under a true fixed-price contract in which the contractor is legally obligated to absorb the financial cost of technical failure, remedy defective designs at its own expense, and deliver a functioning product meeting rigorous technical specifications as a condition precedent to payment—while retaining substantial intellectual property rights to the underlying engineering know-how—the contractor retains the economic risk, rendering the research unfunded and potentially eligible for the credit.
Hypothetical Worked Example: Multi-Phase Aerospace Engineering Lifecycle

To demonstrate the operational mechanics of the 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4) exclusions, the 80% "substantially all" rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), and the post-2021 Section 174 capitalization rules across a single product development lifecycle, the following hypothetical scenario models the multi-phase aerospace engineering operations of AeroTech Solutions. All monetary figures and calculations below are hypothetical and are computed step by step using the statutory rules and amortization periods established in 26 U.S.C. §§ 41 and 174.
Hypothetical Scenario Facts

Assume AeroTech Solutions, a hypothetical domestic aerospace engineering and manufacturing corporation, enters into a strict fixed-price contract during the 2026 tax year (a tax year beginning after December 31, 2021) with a major commercial airline to design, test, and manufacture a proprietary, ultra-lightweight carbon-composite passenger seating mechanism. Under the express terms of the contract, the airline's obligation to make payment is strictly contingent upon the seating mechanism passing Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) dynamic crash-load certification while meeting strict weight reduction tolerances, and AeroTech retains all substantial intellectual property rights, patents, and engineering rights to the resulting seating technology. During the 2026 tax year, AeroTech incurs $1,000,000 in total project expenditures across four sequential operational phases.

In Phase 1 (Domestic Pre-CDR Experimental Design and Destructive Testing), AeroTech incurs $550,000 in domestic engineering wages and destructive pilot-model testing supplies prior to Critical Design Review (CDR) to resolve fundamental technological uncertainty regarding whether the novel carbon-composite lattice architecture can withstand FAA crash loads without structural delamination. Measured on a contemporaneous, reasonable time-tracking basis, 85% of the domestic engineering hours and associated costs in Phase 1 ($467,500) consist of direct iterative computer modeling, finite element stress simulations, and destructive physical testing, while the remaining 15% ($82,500) consist of direct technical supervision and non-excluded supporting engineering documentation.

In Phase 2 (Foreign CAD Subcontracting in Germany), AeroTech seeks to accelerate three-dimensional computer-aided design (CAD) modeling during the pre-CDR development window by paying $150,000 to a specialized aerospace engineering firm that performs all modeling work at its facility in Germany, after which AeroTech's domestic engineers in the United States analyze and integrate the resulting digital data files.

In Phase 3 (Commercial Production Run and Post-Deployment Lever Debugging), following successful FAA crash-load certification and formal CDR design freeze, AeroTech transitions into manufacturing and delivers the initial 1,000 commercial seating units to the airline. One month after commercial deployment, the airline reports that the passenger recline lever intermittently sticks when subjected to extreme cabin temperature fluctuations during high-altitude flight. In response, AeroTech incurs $120,000 in domestic engineering wages to troubleshoot the deployed commercial units and apply a commercially available synthetic lubricant fix without halting production or issuing a formal Engineering Change Proposal (ECP).

In Phase 4 (Customer-Specific Dimensional Adaptation for Second Airline), a second commercial airline observes the commercial success of the certified carbon-composite seats and orders the mechanism for its own aircraft fleet, requesting that the seat frame dimensions be widened by exactly two inches to accommodate a different cabin aisle layout. AeroTech incurs $180,000 in domestic engineering wages to geometrically scale the existing CAD files and alter the production tooling where no new scientific or engineering uncertainty exists regarding the carbon-composite material's structural strength or the core mechanism's mechanical viability.
Step-by-Step Qualification and Exclusion Computation

Evaluating Phase 1 ($550,000) under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), and 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) demonstrates that because the contract is a true fixed-price agreement with payment strictly contingent on passing FAA crash-load certification and AeroTech retains all substantial intellectual property rights, Phase 1 is legally unfunded and is not excluded under Section 41(d)(4)(H). Furthermore, under the "substantially all" requirement of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), at least 80% of a taxpayer's research activities for a business component, measured on a reasonable basis, must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for the business component to qualify. In Phase 1, direct process-of-experimentation activities account for:
Experimentation Ratio = $467,500 / $550,000 = 0.85 (or 85%)

Because the 85% experimentation ratio exceeds the 80% regulatory threshold under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), and because the remaining 15% ($82,500) consists of direct technical supervision and supporting activities that do not fall into any Section 41(d)(4) statutory exclusion, 100% of Phase 1 expenditures ($550,000) qualify as eligible Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) under 26 U.S.C. § 41.

By contrast, Phases 2, 3, and 4 are categorically disqualified from the research credit under three distinct provisions of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4). In Phase 2 ($150,000), because the subcontracted CAD modeling is physically conducted in Germany—outside the geographic territory of the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any U.S. possession—100% of the $150,000 expenditure is statutorily excluded from Section 41 QREs under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(F), even though the resulting engineering data is subsequently evaluated and utilized by domestic engineers in the United States. In Phase 3 ($120,000), because the carbon-composite seating mechanism had already passed FAA certification, cleared CDR, met the taxpayer's basic functional and economic requirements, and entered commercial production through the manufacture and delivery of the first 1,000 commercial units, the $120,000 incurred for post-deployment troubleshooting and lubricant debugging is 100% excluded under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A) as research conducted after the beginning of commercial production. In Phase 4 ($180,000), geometrically scaling the certified seat frame by two inches to fit a second airline customer's cabin layout applies established engineering parameters without confronting new technological uncertainty; consequently, 100% of the $180,000 expenditure is excluded under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(B) as the adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement.
Aggregating the four lifecycle phases yields the following total project expenditure, statutory exclusion, and net QRE computations:
Total Lifecycle Project Expenditure = $550,000 + $150,000 + $120,000 + $180,000 = $1,000,000
Total Section 41(d)(4) Excluded Expenditures = $150,000 + $120,000 + $180,000 = $450,000
Net Eligible Section 41 QREs = $1,000,000 − $450,000 = $550,000

Finally, applying the post-December 31, 2021 mandatory capitalization rules of 26 U.S.C. § 174 illustrates the divergent tax recovery trajectories across the project phases. The $550,000 of domestic experimental expenditures in Phase 1 must be capitalized and amortized ratably over a five-year domestic recovery period, yielding a full-year amortization rate of:
Annual Domestic Section 174 Amortization Rate = $550,000 / 5 = $110,000 per year

Conversely, the $150,000 of foreign research expenditures incurred in Germany during Phase 2—despite being completely disqualified from the Section 41 tax credit under Section 41(d)(4)(F)—still constitute specified research or experimental expenditures under Section 174 and must be capitalized and amortized over a 15-year foreign recovery period, yielding a full-year amortization rate of:
Annual Foreign Section 174 Amortization Rate = $150,000 / 15 = $10,000 per year

body.text: Federal Appellate Jurisprudence Interpreting Section 41(d)(4)

Federal appellate courts have enforced the exclusions of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4) strictly against corporate taxpayers, establishing controlling judicial precedents on commercial production supplies, the intersection of customer adaptation and the "substantially all" rule, and contractual risk allocation under the funded research exclusion.
Commercial Production Supplies: Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner

In Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit addressed the boundary between qualified research supply costs and commercial manufacturing under the rationale of the Section 41(d)(4)(A) commercial production exclusion. Union Carbide conducted large-scale experimental process tests—including the UCAT-J catalyst project—aimed at improving chemical manufacturing efficiency and preventing polyethylene buildup while simultaneously operating its industrial plants to manufacture chemical products for commercial sale. While the IRS conceded that the incremental engineering labor dedicated to the process experiments qualified, the taxpayer sought to claim the entire cost of the raw materials and chemical feedstocks processed during these plant-scale experimental test runs as qualified research supplies.

The Second Circuit affirmed the Tax Court's disallowance, holding that raw materials used in manufacturing finished goods for commercial sale do not constitute supplies used in the conduct of qualified research when those raw material costs would have been incurred regardless of whether process experimentation occurred concurrently. Because the chemical feedstocks were purchased for and converted into salable commercial inventory destined for the marketplace—rather than being consumed exclusively in a non-commercial pilot model or isolated experimental trial—they fell outside the protective scope of Section 41. Union Carbide establishes a firm judicial precedent that conducting concurrent process experimentation on an active commercial production line does not convert ordinary manufacturing raw materials or post-commercialization production inputs into qualified research expenditures.
Substantially All Experimentation vs. Adaptation: Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner

In Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), affirming T.C. Memo. 2021-15, the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit clarified how the 80% "substantially all" requirement of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) interacts with the Section 41(d)(4) exclusions for customer adaptation and commercial production. The taxpayer, through its commercial shipbuilding subsidiary Corn Island Shipyard, claimed R&D tax credits for the engineering and construction of two first-of-their-kind marine vessels: a new floating dry dock and a customized tank barge.

Under the quantitative fraction established in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), at least 80% of a taxpayer's research activities for a business component, measured on a reasonable basis (typically employee time or cost), must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for the activity to qualify. Crucially, the regulation provides that only if that strict 80% threshold is met can the remaining 20% of activities be included in the qualified pool, and even then, only to the extent the remaining activities are not excluded under Section 41(d)(4). Furthermore, direct production activities and excluded customer adaptation hours that are not part of the experimental process dilute the numerator of the 80% fraction when included in the project scope. In Little Sandy Coal, the taxpayer relied on retrospective, arbitrary time estimates and generalized post-facto trial testimony rather than contemporaneous project accounting, failing to provide a verifiable denominator or numerator proving that at least 80% of employee activities involved true scientific experimentation rather than routine marine fabrication or customer customization.

The Seventh Circuit emphasized a vital doctrinal distinction that directly reinforces Section 41(d)(4)(B): building a custom-ordered vessel—which inherently adapts established naval engineering principles to a specific client's spatial, draft, and weight specifications—does not automatically equate to a process of experimentation resolving technological uncertainty. Generalized novelty, first-time fabrication of a custom product, and high-level retrospective time estimates are legally insufficient to defeat an IRS determination that engineering activities represent routine production or excluded customer adaptation under Section 41(d)(4)(B).
Funded Research Doctrine: Fairchild, Geosyntec, and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson

Federal appellate decisions governing the funded research exclusion under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) rely on a granular examination of contractual risk allocation and payment remedies. The baseline appellate standard was established by the Federal Circuit in Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), which evaluated a defense contractor's fixed-price incentive contract with the United States Air Force to develop the T-46A Next Generation Trainer aircraft. The Federal Circuit held that because the contract's financing provisions required Fairchild to return progress payments unless it successfully delivered contractually compliant prototypes passing rigorous technical specifications, the contractor's right to retain payment was strictly contingent upon the successful development of the specified product. Because Fairchild bore the financial risk of technical failure, the research was legally unfunded under Section 41(d)(4)(H).

The Eleventh Circuit refined this contractual risk-allocation doctrine in Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), involving a specialty consulting and environmental engineering firm operating under both fixed-price contracts and capped cost-plus contracts. While agreeing with the lower court that true fixed-price contracts inherently place maximum economic risk on the contractor—who must absorb cost overruns and remedy failed performance without additional compensation—the Eleventh Circuit reversed the lower court with respect to the capped cost-plus contracts. Under those capped cost-plus agreements, clients were contractually obligated to reimburse Geosyntec for performing predefined tasks at predefined hourly rates up to a budgetary ceiling, without requiring Geosyntec to guarantee the ultimate technical success of the environmental remediation design. Because payment depended on task performance rather than experimental success, the Eleventh Circuit held that the capped cost-plus projects placed primary financial risk on the client, rendering them "funded" and excluded under Section 41(d)(4)(H).

Subsequently, in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner (8th Cir. May 2024), the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit reaffirmed this strict contractual analysis by denying a structural engineering firm's R&D credit claim in its entirety. Although the structural engineering firm's contracts required its designs to conform with professional standards of care and complex building and design codes, the Eighth Circuit concluded that general professional liability standards and code compliance obligations lacked the contractual specificity required to make payment strictly contingent upon the success of experimental research. Because the firm was compensated for delivering standard structural design deliverables rather than assuming the financial risk of failed scientific experimentation, the court held that the engineering work was funded by the clients and categorically excluded under Section 41(d)(4)(H).
State-Level Conformity and Executive Enforcement of Section 41(d)(4) Exclusions

Because the vast majority of U.S. states offering corporate R&D tax incentives structurally tether their state tax statutes to the definitions in IRC § 41, state departments of revenue and administrative tax tribunals actively enforce the federal exclusions of Section 41(d)(4) and federal appellate precedents to disallow localized state tax credit claims.

body.text: Idaho: Application of Little Sandy Coal to Architectural and Software Adaptation

Under Idaho Code § 63-3029G, Idaho directly incorporates the federal definitions, four-part test, and statutory exclusions of IRC § 41 into the Idaho Credit for Research Activities. In an administrative protest decided by the Idaho State Tax Commission (Docket No. 1-707-713-536 and Document 0-832-082-944), an Idaho S-corporation engaged in developing residential real estate floorplans, residential construction engineering models, and custom architectural software claimed the Idaho R&D tax credit based on an externally commissioned third-party tax study. Following a complete disallowance by the Idaho Income Tax Audit Bureau, the Idaho State Tax Commission upheld the denial in full by pointing explicitly to the Section 41(d)(4)(A) exclusion for research conducted after the beginning of commercial production and the Section 41(d)(4)(B) exclusion for customer adaptation.

Relying directly on the Seventh Circuit's holding in Little Sandy Coal, the Idaho State Tax Commission determined that the taxpayer's reliance on unverified, high-level percentage time estimates failed to substantiate a genuine process of experimentation or establish the 80% "substantially all" threshold. The Commission concluded that modifying residential architectural floorplans and structural home models to accommodate specific buyer preferences or lot dimensions constituted routine commercial home design and customer-specific adaptation barred under Section 41(d)(4)(B), rather than experimental research resolving fundamental engineering uncertainty.
Texas: Rulemaking Litigation Over Evolutionary Research and Internal Use Software

In Texas, the state legislature enacted R&D sales tax exemptions and franchise tax credits to make the state economically competitive in attracting high-technology investment, explicitly benchmarking its tax incentives against rival technology hubs such as California and Massachusetts during legislative committee hearings. However, regulatory amendments promulgated by the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts under Title 34 of the Texas Administrative Code (34 TAC §§ 3.340 and 3.599) triggered administrative litigation (Ryan, LLC v. Glenn Hegar, Cause No. D-1-GN-21-006290) regarding the executive branch's authority to narrow the interpretation of "qualified research" and expand the Section 41(d)(4)(E) internal use software exclusion.

Corporate taxpayers challenged the Texas Comptroller's attempt to enforce an administrative standard requiring research to be inherently "innovative" or "cutting-edge" to qualify, arguing that such a bright-line restriction unlawfully expanded the exclusionary net of Section 41(d)(4) beyond the federal Treasury Regulations incorporated by the Texas statute. As the challengers emphasized, federal Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4 expressly confirms that evolutionary technological advances qualify for the credit without needing to expand or refine the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the field, provided the activities do not fall into a specific Section 41(d)(4) exclusion. Taxpayers simultaneously contested the Comptroller's restrictive treatment of internal use software under Section 41(d)(4)(E), asserting that internal software projects satisfying the federal three-part High Threshold of Innovation Test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6) must qualify under state rules to prevent dual compliance burdens and align with the legislature's mandate of statutory conformity with IRC § 41.
Indiana: Enforcement of Geosyntec Against Commercial Warranty Clauses

The Indiana Department of Revenue similarly enforces the federal funded research exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) through rigorous line-by-line contract analysis. In a published administrative ruling (45 25-183 / IARP 20250430-IR-045250183NRA), the Indiana Department of Revenue denied a corporate manufacturer's R&D credit claim in full by directly applying the Eleventh Circuit's federal Geosyntec precedent to the taxpayer's customer purchase orders and operational agreements.

During the administrative protest, the taxpayer argued that its research was unfunded because its customer contracts contained inspection and acceptance clauses permitting buyers to reject delivery if the manufactured products were defective in material or workmanship or failed to meet basic dimensional requirements. The Indiana Department of Revenue rejected this argument, ruling that standard commercial warranty and inspection clauses governing defective workmanship do not make payment contingent upon the technical success of experimental research. Because the contracts governed the sale of custom commercial goods and failed to shift the financial risk of failed scientific experimentation onto the seller under the Geosyntec standard, the Department held that the underlying engineering activities were funded by the customers and statutorily excluded under Section 41(d)(4)(H).
Technical Literacy and Specialist Compliance Architecture

The convergence of strict statutory exclusions under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4), post-2021 Section 174 capitalization exposure, stringent judicial substantiation standards under Little Sandy Coal, and aggressive state-level audits creates technical substantiation challenges that generalist accounting practices are frequently unequipped to defend. When an IRS engineer or state field examiner asserts that a specific project constitutes excluded post-CDR debugging under Section 41(d)(4)(A), routine customer adaptation under Section 41(d)(4)(B), or general and administrative internal use software under Section 41(d)(4)(E), defending the claim requires granular technical fluency in the underlying low-level physics, metallurgy, computer numerical control (CNC) machining variables, distributed software architecture, or biomedical sciences. Generalist financial auditors often lack the domain vocabulary required to distinguish an iterative finite-element simulation resolving structural uncertainty from a routine CAD geometry adjustment performed for a specific client order.

This domain-specific engineering literacy enables specialist advisors to conduct peer-to-peer technical interviews with a corporate client's lead engineers and project managers, isolating the exact chronological and technical boundary at which a project transitions from a valid process of experimentation under Section 41(d)(1) into excluded commercial production under Section 41(d)(4)(A) or customer adaptation under Section 41(d)(4)(B).
Conclusions

The statutory exclusions codified in 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A)–(H) and implemented through Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c) serve as the decisive legal boundary separating federally subsidized technological experimentation from routine commercial engineering, offshore subcontracting, and standard business operations. Across the federal appellate circuits and state taxing authorities, administrative and judicial enforcement has converged around three uncompromising legal principles. First, under Section 41(d)(4)(A), the IRS Aerospace ATG, and the Second Circuit's precedent in Union Carbide, any engineering labor, post-deployment debugging, or raw material supply expenditure incurred after a business component clears Critical Design Review, achieves functional readiness, or enters commercial production is categorically barred unless a formal engineering redesign halts production to resolve newly discovered technological uncertainty. Second, under the Seventh Circuit's holding in Little Sandy Coal and parallel state tribunal enforcement such as Idaho's administrative rulings, corporate taxpayers cannot rely on retrospective time estimates or generalized product customization to satisfy the 80% "substantially all" process-of-experimentation threshold against a Section 41(d)(4)(B) customer adaptation challenge. Third, under Fairchild, Geosyntec, Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, and state revenue rulings in jurisdictions such as Indiana, contractual arrangements that reimburse hourly tasks under capped cost-plus terms, rely on standard commercial workmanship warranties, or fail to make payment explicitly contingent on the technical success of experimental research are disqualified as funded research under Section 41(d)(4)(H).

When these strict Section 41(d)(4) exclusions are coupled with mandatory five-year domestic and 15-year foreign capitalization and amortization under 26 U.S.C. § 174 for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021, the compliance stakes for corporate taxpayers are substantially elevated. To withstand federal and state examination, taxpayers and their advisors must abandon retrospective percentage estimation in favor of contemporaneous, technically literate project accounting that maps engineering activities to discrete stage-gate milestones, audits third-party customer contracts for explicit risk-allocation terms, and systematically strips out Section 41(d)(4) excluded activities at the sub-project level prior to filing.
